chunks: "A stepper motor works by moving a magnetic field in small jumps and letting the rotor chase it.
The stator has coils arranged in phases; the rotor is a permanent magnet or a toothed iron piece.
If I energise one coil, it creates a magnetic pole and the rotor rotates until its nearest tooth or opposite pole lines up with it, and it stays there.
If I then switch off that coil and energise the next one, the equilibrium position moves by one step, and the rotor turns to it.
Repeating the sequence A, B, A-bar, B-bar rotates the shaft one step at a time; reversing the sequence reverses direction.
In a typical hybrid motor with two phases and 50 rotor teeth, one full cycle of the sequence moves the rotor one tooth pitch, 7. 2 degrees, in four 1. 8 degree steps.
Energising both phases at once, full-step, gives the most torque.
Alternating one then two phases gives half steps, and driving the two phase currents as a sine and a cosine, microstepping, lets the rotor settle between teeth for smoother motion.
Position control is open loop: I count the pulses. That works as long as the motor produces enough torque to follow.

The torque falls with speed because the coil inductance slows the current rise, and back-EMF grows with speed, which is why drivers use a high supply voltage with current chopping, so the current can reach its rated value quickly.
If the load or acceleration exceeds the available torque, the rotor falls out of step and loses position, with no warning."
